primary.title: India's 17% US tariff relief comes with a catch
primary.description: New Delhi: The US proposal to impose additional tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods, with the possibility of reducing the rate to 17% if the two countries conclude a reciprocal trade agreement, may offer little competitive advantage to engineering goods exporters. Gems and jewellery exporters, meanwhile, expect disruptions to order flows and pressure on margins amid continued uncertainty over market access.Textile exporters said a 17% tariff would place India in a relatively favourable position against certain Asian economies, where corresponding rates are indicated at 18-20%. However, frequent changes in tariff policies and regulations are creating uncertainty for exporters and their overseas buyers.Also Read: Even 17% tariff under India-US trade deal may offer little competitive advantage to Indian exporters: FIEOEngineering goods exporters said even a 17% rate would not provide a significant competitive advantage, as India would continue to face a tariff disadvantage compared with Bangladesh and Malaysia, among others. "The US accounts for the largest share of India's exports of toys and sports goods, so any increase in US tariffs will directly affect the sector. The proposed duty increase to 25% (17% if a trade deal is concluded), would hurt our competitiveness against other sourcing countries," said Tarun Dewan, executive director, Sports Goods Export Promotion Council.Under the current US tariff structure, Bangladesh faces a tariff of around 18%, which could rise to 20% if its consultations with the Trump administration fail. Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia also face tariffs of 18%, with a fallback rate of 25% if their negotiations fail. Vietnam is proposed to face a tariff of 20% under the arrangement and up to 35% without one."If India is at 17% under a trade deal with the US, I am not entirely sure that gives us a significant competitive advantage as India would continue to face a tariff disadvantage against certain economies," said Pankaj Chadha, chairman, EEPC India.The tariffs are scheduled to come into effect in January next year.Kirit Bhansali, chairman of the Gem and Jewellery Export Promotion Council (GJEPC), said India's gems and jewellery sector had faced prolonged uncertainty over US tariff measures, with duties ranging from 5.5% to 50%, putting pressure on exports, payment cycles and logistics costs. "Tariffs raise landed costs and retail prices, potentially dampening US consumer demand and affecting jobs and businesses across the value chain in both countries... the proposed 25% US tariff on Indian goods could again weigh on the sector," Bhansali said.Also Read: India, China and others aren't taking Trump's latest tariff salvo lying downChadha added that it was too early to draw conclusions about the competitiveness of India's engineering sector in the US market following the implementation of the proposed tariff.Exporters have sought a stable and predictable tariff framework with the US to sustain trade growth and build long-term business relationships. They said frequent changes were difficult to accommodate in ongoing commercial negotiations, pricing arrangements and buyer commitments, particularly in the textile and apparel sector, where orders are often negotiated and finalised well before shipment. "The proposed 17% rate, if realised through a trade agreement, would place India at a relatively favourable position vis-a-vis selected competing Asian economies, where the corresponding rates are indicated at 18-20%. This could offer Indian textile and apparel exporters a measure of competitive advantage in the US market," said the Confederation of Indian Textile Industry.Exporters said that summer orders booked until February are unlikely to be hit.
